name: functional-core-imperative-shell
intent: Split a unit of code into a pure functional core that turns values into decisions and a thin imperative shell that gathers the world, calls the core and carries out its decision, so the business rules can be reasoned about and tested without I/O or test doubles.
problem: A module mixes decision logic with I/O: the rules for what should happen are interleaved with reading the database, reading the clock, logging, and writing back - so every branch is reachable only through a live environment, the behaviour is verifiable only with mocks or an end-to-end test, and the same rule gets re-implemented in each entry point that needs it.
context: Applies wherever a unit both decides and does: request handlers, CLI commands, batch jobs, protocol and reconciliation loops, UI stores, domain services that already know about a repository. It needs a place where inputs can be gathered before the decision and effects applied after it (an entry point, a handler, a composition root), and it pays off most where the decision space is large relative to the I/O - combinatorially rich rules over a small set of already-loaded values - while I/O-dominated code should be left alone.
benefits: The rules become ordinary pure functions: same values in, same decision out, verified by table-driven or property tests with no mocks, no container and no clock to fake.
Effects are concentrated in one thin layer, which makes them auditable: what leaves the process (writes, messages, payments, emails) is visible in the shell instead of scattered through the logic.
The core is independent of infrastructure, so the same decisions are reused behind different entry points (HTTP, CLI, queue consumer, batch) and survive framework and storage swaps.
Reasoning is local: a reader can evaluate a rule from its inputs and outputs alone, and the shell has few conditionals, so the program's progression over time is easy to follow.
A large share of the code base becomes deterministic and safe to run concurrently by construction, which shrinks the combination space that integration tests have to cover down to the wiring.
Making non-determinism explicit (now, ids, flags, already-fetched data as parameters) exposes hidden dependencies that were previously implicit in the code.
tradeoffs: The boundary is unenforced convention in most languages: nothing stops a core function from calling the clock, a repository or a logger, so the split decays unless it is policed mechanically (import checks in CI, a no_std core crate, effect types, review).
The shell becomes the code that grows: workflows, orchestration branches and 'just one lookup' creep in until the shell is the god object and the decisions it holds are as untestable as before.
Forcing the split where the logic is I/O all the way down (streaming copies, adapters that only translate calls) adds a layer of ceremony and indirection with no testability gain.

Passing values instead of mutating them means more copying and more data threaded through signatures; on large payloads or hot loops those extra passes cost real time, and sometimes force an effect-description layer just to keep the shell branch-free.

Decisions as data: returning 'what should happen' (new state, events, effect descriptions) instead of doing it grows the core's return types and needs a matcher/interpreter in the shell, which is how code bases drift into maintaining a small effect system.
From the entry point the core is nearly invisible - often a single function call - so reviewers systematically overestimate how much logic the shell holds and where the complexity really lives.

participants.responsibility: Pure functions and immutable values that hold all the decisions: they compute new values, events or effect descriptions from their inputs, never read or write anything outside themselves, and never call the shell.

The only place effects happen: it reads the world (database, network, files, clock, randomness), hands the gathered values to the core, and applies the returned decision. It owns orchestration and error handling but no business rules.

The plain data the shell extracts before the decision (already-fetched records, injected now, ids, flags) together with the value types the core works on; making the world explicit as a value is what allows the core to be pure.
The core's result - new state, a domain event, an acceptance/rejection, or a description of effects - returned as a value so the shell has to execute rather than interpret it.

The implementation side of the boundary (repository, gateway, clock, notifier, logger). Ports may be declared by the core but are implemented and wired outside it; the core never depends on an implementation.
main or the framework handler: it wires the adapters, starts the shell's orchestration, and is the single place that knows both the core and the concrete infrastructure.

use_cases: Request handlers: gather (load entities, resolve the caller, take the current time), call one pure decision function, then write back and publish events - the handler keeps no rules of its own.

Pricing, billing and entitlement decisions: a pure function over a cart or subscription plus a date returns the charge, discount and proration, so money rules are verified in table tests instead of through a service and a database.

Validation and normalisation at the edges: parsing untrusted input into domain values through smart constructors is pure, while the shell decides where the bytes came from and what to do with the failures.

Schedulers, controllers and reconcilers: the loop computes the desired effects from a snapshot of current state (Kubernetes-style reconcile, sync jobs, sagas, outbox flushes) and an executor applies them, which makes the controller testable without the cluster or the queue.

UI and application state: a reducer (state + action -> new state) is the functional core, while the store/object layer holds the state, talks to the network and performs the effects in unidirectional flow.

Domain services in an existing layered application: keep the aggregate and its rules pure and let the application service become the shell that loads, decides and saves, without introducing a new architecture.

CQRS command handlers and Event Sourcing projections: the command handler is a shell that loads the aggregate, calls a pure transition function, and persists events; the projection is a pure fold over an event stream.

DDD aggregates and domain events: the aggregate's state transitions are pure functions, serialised by the shell; the same aggregate logic is reused in synchronous REST handlers and asynchronous message consumers.

FaaS and serverless functions: each invocation is a shell that fetches its inputs from a queue or KV store, calls the pure core, and writes the result back - cold-start time is spent on I/O, not on test setup.

Microservices adopting strangler-fig migration: new behaviour is added as a pure core behind a feature flag or router; the shell handles the old and new code paths side-by-side until the old path is retired.

Event-driven systems and outbox patterns: the shell reads a message, calls a pure handler that returns a list of effects (persist, publish, email), and the shell executes them inside a transaction or outbox relay.

Redux applications: reducers are a pure state-transition core (state plus action to new state), while middleware performs asynchronous work and other side effects around dispatch; the official Redux guidance makes the reducer/middleware boundary explicit.

Kubernetes controllers: the reconciliation loop reads observed and desired resource state, computes the next change as a decision, and uses the API server to apply effects; the controller documentation is a production example of separating state-based decisions from cluster I/O.
avoid_when: The code is I/O all the way down - a stream copy, a repository adapter that only translates calls, a thin proxy: leave it imperative and test it at the integration level.
The logic is a handful of lines with one branch used from a single place: an inline condition in the handler is simpler than a core/shell pair plus a new module.
A performance-critical inner loop where separating reads from computation forces extra passes or copies over large data; interleaving I/O and computation is sometimes the only efficient shape.

The decision needs data discovered in sequence (query, decide, query again): gather everything up front where possible, or accept an effect-description layer - but do not call the core pure while it queries through a callback.

The framework already provides the seam and the team follows it (ASP.NET filters, Ktor/Spring pipelines, Redux reducers, actor behaviours) and the logic is small: follow that shape instead of building a second structure beside it.
anti_patterns: Impure core: the core takes a repository or database handle 'just to look something up', or calls the clock and logger inside a rule, so tests need mocks again and the split bought nothing.
Shell with decisions: business conditionals migrate into the handler (per-endpoint premium-user checks), so the same rule is duplicated per entry point and only testable through the transport.
Boolean oracle: the core returns true/false or a flag and the shell interprets it, splitting the decision back across both sides of the boundary.
Universal purity: refactoring single-input helpers into core/shell pairs, or wrapping every call in an effect type, until the code is a ceremony of adapters with no logic worth isolating.
Logging, metrics or tracing inside the decision functions - the most common accidental effect, invisible in review and fatal to deterministic tests.
Mutating the caller's data from a 'pure' function (sorting the argument in place, appending to it) so the shell's state changes behind its back and aliasing bugs return through the front door.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: deciding and executing are different responsibilities with different reasons to change and different test strategies.
Referential transparency / the functional interaction law: a pure function must not invoke an impure activity, so effects may only be called from the shell.
Dependency inversion: dependencies point inward; the core may declare what it needs as data or ports, but the implementations are injected at the composition root.
Immutability and value semantics: decisions are values, updated by producing new values, so state cannot change behind a caller's back.
Single responsibility: the shell reads, calls and writes; the core decides. A function that does both is the failure mode this pattern removes.
Explicit inputs: everything non-deterministic (time, randomness, ids, flags, environment) becomes a parameter, which makes hidden dependencies visible.
best_practices: Make every non-deterministic input a parameter (now, ids, flags, already-fetched data) instead of reaching out from the core.
Return decisions, not verdicts: new state plus the events or effects to perform, so the shell has nothing to interpret.
Keep the shell free of domain branching; if a conditional in the shell depends on domain state, it belongs in the core.
Enforce the boundary mechanically - keep the core import-clean (CI import check, a no_std crate, an effects module, a lint rule, or an AST-based effect audit tool) - because convention alone decays.
Test the core with table-driven or property tests and no mocks; keep a few integration tests for the shell's wiring.

Decompose the shell when it grows: a shell function with more than a couple of independent effects should be split into smaller read/apply steps (or an effect description) before it becomes the new god object.
Do not apply the pattern to I/O-dominated code or one-branch helpers; an unfavourable pure/impure ratio is the most common misjudgement.

Model errors as data inside the core: use Result, Either or discriminated-union failure types returned as values, not exceptions thrown from the core; the shell pattern-matches on the result and handles all side effects.

Enforce the no-std or no-IO constraint in the core crate with a build script or CI lint (effect-audit for Rust, clj-kondo for Clojure, import linters for other languages) to catch accidental Clock, Logger or Repository calls.

For the core's return type, prefer a structured decision value (new state + domain events + side-effect descriptions) over a boolean or flag, so the shell never has to interpret a raw primitive to decide what to do.
When the core needs to compose multiple pure functions, use function composition (fold, chain, pipe) rather than introducing an implicit sequence of effects; keep the composition itself pure.

Use property-based testing (Fast-Check, Hypothesis, ScalaCheck) for the core instead of only example-based tests: it exercises edge cases (empty lists, boundary integers, malformed input) that hand-written tables miss.

Isolate deterministic chaos: avoid HashMap, HashSet or other non-deterministic collections inside the core unless the seed is passed in as a parameter; prefer BTreeMap, BTreeSet or sorted alternatives to keep test runs reproducible.
In languages with an effect system (Eff, Freestanding, IO type), model the shell's effects explicitly so the type system enforces what the linter checks by convention.
sources: Gary Bernhardt, Functional Core, Imperative Shell (Destroy All Software screencast, 2012) - the pattern's origin: a functional core managing tweets, cursors and rendering surrounded by a shell of imperative code that manipulates stdin, stdout, the database and the network.
Gary Bernhardt, Boundaries (SCNA 2012 talk) - simple values as the boundaries between components; the same core/shell idea, in the version where a pure core is tested with no test doubles.

Mark Seemann, Functional architecture: a definition (2018) - the functional interaction law: a pure function cannot invoke an impure activity; a functional architecture is code that obeys it with a significant portion of pure code.
Mark Seemann, Functional architecture is Ports and Adapters (2016) - the pattern's place among hexagonal/onion architectures and how Haskell's IO type enforces the boundary.

Mark Seemann, A restaurant sandwich (2024) - the Impureim Sandwich variant of the pattern applied to REST endpoints; demonstrates pure function composition with LINQ/SelectMany and Either-based error handling in C#.
Mark Seemann, What's a sandwich? (2023) - maximising pure code between two impurity phases; validation as a pure parsing phase, impurity kept at the outer boundaries.

Mark Seemann, Dependency inversion without inversion of control (2025) - how the Functional Core, Imperative Shell achieves dependency inversion without Inversion of Control or Dependency Injection containers.

A primer on functional architecture (Increment, 2020) - functional architecture as the natural outcome of keeping the business core pure; alignment with hexagonal/ports-and-adapters patterns; pure core enables deterministic unit testing.

Functional Software Architecture (functional-architecture.org) - two-part architecture: pure functional core implementing domain logic without side effects, and a thin imperative shell handling all side effects and external interactions.

Functional Core, Imperative Shell, Explained (CodeSnatch, 2025) - actionable guidance on the pure/impure split, shell-god failure mode, over-engineering CRUD endpoints, and treating purity as a spectrum not a binary.

Functional core, imperative shell – principledcraft.dev - 80% of bugs live in business logic, so keeping that logic in the pure core enables fast, reliable unit tests; pragmatic caveats on performance overhead and interactive/stateful systems.

René Dekkers, Functional Core, Imperative Shell in C# (2025) - core returns a Result<T> (success/failure with domain events), shell performs persistence and messaging only on success; DateTime.UtcNow passed as a parameter.

Mario Bittencourt, A Look at the Functional Core and Imperative Shell Pattern (SSENSE-TECH, Medium, 2022) - practical application combining FCIS with clean architecture; shell orchestrates input, core decides, shell applies side effects.

Rico Fritzsche, Applying Functional Core and Imperative Shell in Practice (2024) - real-world FCIS adoption: pure domain logic vs. IO-heavy shell; test pyramid with thousands of fast core unit tests, a handful of integration tests for wiring.

Rico Fritzsche, Simplicity Wins: Command Context Consistency (2024) - CQRS and Event Sourcing naturally pair with FCIS; the core makes deterministic state transitions and emits events; the imperative shell handles I/O and side effects.

Alexander Granin, Functional Design and Architecture (Manning, 2020) - FP-first software design; free monads for modelling domain behaviour; property-based and functional testing strategies for the pure core.

Hexagonal Architecture and Functional Core / Imperative Shell (Socratopia, Software Engineering Craft) - FC/IS tightens hexagonal: the core is pure (no side effects, no I/O) while all effects and mutation live in a thin imperative shell; testing guidance for the clean pyramid.

igouss/effect-audit (GitHub) - a Rust tool that parses crates via syn and flags effectful call sites at the domain's boundaries; detects clock-like/nondeterministic sources (SystemTime, random seeds) even via macros; supports no_std enforcement.
zeno-fcis-core (crates.io) - a Rust library family for strict functional-core/imperative-shell enforcement with no_std support, immutable state transitions, and atomic shell interpretation.
